# DelegateMQ

DelegateMQ is a C++17 library with a header-only core that invokes any callable (free function, member function, static function, lambda) synchronously, asynchronously across threads, or remotely across process/network boundaries — all through a single unified API. The same `dmq::MakeDelegate()` syntax works regardless of invocation mode; switching between sync, async, or remote is a one-line change.

## Core Abstractions

### Delegates

- `dmq::Delegate<Sig>` — synchronous, direct call on the caller's thread
- `dmq::DelegateAsync<Sig>` — non-blocking async, fire-and-forget to a target thread
- `dmq::DelegateAsyncWait<Sig>` — blocking async, waits for return value with optional timeout
- `dmq::DelegateRemote<Sig>` — remote invocation, serializes arguments over a transport

All four share the same `dmq::MakeDelegate()` factory and `operator()` invocation syntax.

### Delegate Containers

- `dmq::Signal<Sig>` — thread-safe multicast signal with RAII disconnect via `dmq::ScopedConnection`; the preferred pub/sub primitive
- `dmq::MulticastDelegateSafe<Sig>` — thread-safe broadcast without RAII (manual `+=` / `-=`)
- `dmq::UnicastDelegate<Sig>` / `dmq::UnicastDelegateSafe<Sig>` — single-slot variants

### DataBus (DDS Lite)

- `dmq::databus::DataBus` — topic-based publish/subscribe middleware, location-transparent across threads and remote nodes
- `dmq::databus::Participant` — represents a remote node; bridges local and remote topics
- `dmq::databus::QoS` — per-subscription quality-of-service: Last Value Cache (LVC), Lifespan, Min Separation
- `dmq::databus::DeadlineSubscription<T>` — deadline monitoring: detects a publisher that goes silent (needs `Timer::ProcessTimers()`)

### Ports & Interfaces

The implementations of the interfaces below, in `src/delegate-mq/port` (OS, transport, serializer), form the DelegateMQ Abstraction Layer.

- `dmq::IThread` — cross-platform thread dispatch interface; pre-built ports for stdlib, Win32, POSIX (raw pthreads), FreeRTOS, ThreadX, Zephyr, CMSIS-RTOS2, NuttX, Qt, and bare-metal (ARM/RISC-V)
- `dmq::ISerializer<Sig>` — serialization interface; adapters for MessagePack, RapidJSON, Cereal, Bitsery
- `dmq::transport::ITransport` — transport interface; adapters for ZeroMQ, NNG, MQTT, TCP/UDP, serial, pipes
- `dmq::IDispatcher` — dispatches serialized data to remote endpoints

## Key API Patterns

### Synchronous delegate

```cpp
auto sync = dmq::MakeDelegate(&obj, &MyClass::Method);
sync(args);
```

### Asynchronous non-blocking (fire-and-forget)

```cpp
dmq::os::Thread worker("Worker");
worker.CreateThread();
auto async = dmq::MakeDelegate(&obj, &MyClass::Method, worker);
async(args);  // queued to worker; caller returns immediately
```

### Asynchronous blocking (with return value)

```cpp
auto asyncWait = dmq::MakeDelegate(&obj, &MyClass::Method, worker, dmq::WAIT_INFINITE);
ReturnType result = asyncWait(args);  // caller blocks until worker completes
```

### Signal / slot

```cpp
dmq::Signal<void(int)> OnEvent;
auto conn = OnEvent.Connect(dmq::MakeDelegate(&obj, &Listener::Handle, thread));
OnEvent(42);  // conn auto-disconnects when it goes out of scope
```

### Remote delegate

```cpp
// Receiver: bind a handler to the shared message ID
dmq::RemoteChannel<void(int)> rx(transport, serializer);
rx.Bind(this, &Class::Handler, MSG_ID);
dispatcher.RegisterEndpoint(MSG_ID, rx.GetEndpoint());  // dispatcher: dmq::rpc::RemoteDispatcher

// Sender: pass the ID to the constructor — no Bind() needed
dmq::RemoteChannel<void(int)> tx(transport, serializer, MSG_ID);
tx(42);  // serialized and sent over the network
```

`dmq::rpc::RemoteDispatcher` (`extras/rpc/`) is what an application holds to use `RemoteChannel` — it owns the network thread, the receive loop, and ACK/retry-status routing. Key methods: `Attach(sendTransport, recvTransport)`, `AttachRetryMonitor(retryMonitor)`, `SetCloseHandler(handler)`, `RegisterEndpoint(id, endpoint)`, `Start()`/`Stop()`, `RemoteInvokeWait(channel, args...)`.

### DataBus publish/subscribe

```cpp
auto conn = dmq::databus::DataBus::Subscribe<float>(
    "sensor/temp", [](const float& v) { use(v); }, &workerThread);  // IThread*; omit for sync
dmq::databus::DataBus::Publish<float>("sensor/temp", 25.5f);
```

## Threading and Async Model

- The core library creates no threads; every thread is explicitly constructed by the application. The exceptions are opt-in helpers that each own one receive thread: `dmq::databus::NetworkNode` and `dmq::rpc::RemoteDispatcher`.
- Async delegates are queued to the target thread's priority queue; the thread's `Process()` loop dequeues and invokes.
- Non-blocking async (`DelegateAsync`) copies all arguments so the caller can return immediately without stack lifetime risk: by-value arguments are stored in the message (one copy, as for a sync call), and the data behind reference and pointer arguments is copied to the heap.
- Blocking async (`DelegateAsyncWait`) passes arguments on the stack; the caller blocks until the target thread completes.
- Thread constructor parameters `threadName` and `cpuName` are `const char*` at the binary interface (with `std::string` inline overloads).
- Thread queue full policy is configurable per thread via `dmq::FullPolicy` (aliased as `dmq::os::FullPolicy`): `DROP` (discard), `TIMEOUT` (wait then drop), or `FAULT` (assert/halt, the default).
- Thread queue size: `maxQueueSize = 0` (the default) means the port's default size (`dmq::DEFAULT_QUEUE_SIZE` on RTOS ports and Qt, `dmq::THREAD_DESKTOP_QUEUE_SIZE` on stdlib/Win32/POSIX), never unbounded.
- Synchronized start: an optional `dmq::os::StartGate`, set with `Thread::SetStartGate(&gate)` before `CreateThread()`, holds any number of threads ready but processing nothing (at any priority) until `gate.Open()` releases them together. Available on every thread port (`DMQ_HAS_START_GATE`), not bare metal. See [PORTING](docs/PORTING.md#start-gate-synchronized-start).
- Thread exit behavior is configurable via `dmq::ExitPolicy`: `DRAIN` (default; invoke every message queued before `ExitThread()`) or `DISCARD` (drop queued messages; blocked `DelegateAsyncWait` senders are cancelled rather than left waiting).

## Object Lifetime Safety

- **Raw pointer targets**: unsafe for non-blocking async — object may be destroyed before the queued callback executes.
- **`std::shared_ptr` targets**: safe — delegate holds a `weak_ptr`; if the object is destroyed before dispatch the callback is silently skipped, no crash.
- **Singletons / globals**: safe because their lifetime exceeds any thread.
- Never call `shared_from_this()` in a destructor when delegates are involved.

## Known Constraints and Gotchas

- `DelegateAsync` (fire-and-forget) does not return the target function's return value. Use `DelegateAsyncWait` for blocking with return, or `Signal` for broadcast callbacks.
- Out-parameters (pointer or reference arguments modified by the handler) are not reflected back to the caller for non-blocking async; deep-copying is one-way. Use blocking async if out-parameters are needed.
- C-style array arguments decay to pointers per the C standard; pass `std::vector` or a struct instead.
- Passing a `std::shared_ptr` argument through an async delegate copies the smart pointer, not the pointed-to object — the pointed-to data is shared, not duplicated.
- `Signal::Connect()` and every `Subscribe*()` return a `[[nodiscard]]` `dmq::ScopedConnection` that owns the subscription. Discarding it disconnects immediately: no callbacks, no error. Store it in a member variable or container.
- Each DataBus topic has exactly one C++ type; a type mismatch between publisher and subscriber triggers a fault at runtime.
- `Signal` is thread-safe for concurrent connect/disconnect/emit, but a synchronous subscriber connected to a `Signal` runs inline on the emitting thread (potential priority inversion).
- Message dispatch order on a thread: `HIGH` priority messages run before `NORMAL` ones; within each priority, FIFO. Use explicit sequencing if ordering across multiple sources matters.
- Don't delete a `dmq::os::Thread` from one of its own callbacks: on ThreadX and Zephyr it faults, since the thread's stack can't be freed while it runs on it. Call `ExitThread()` from the callback and delete the object from another thread.
- **LVC rewind (out-of-order delivery):** when a subscriber connects to a Last Value Cache topic with a worker thread, it may receive a fresh live value followed by a stale cached value delivered slightly late. The DataBus dispatches the LVC value outside its internal lock to prevent deadlocks, which opens a narrow window for a concurrent publisher to push a newer value first. The fix is an application-level sequence number: embed a `uint32_t seq` in every message (stamp it at publish time with an atomic counter) and guard the subscriber with `dmq::util::MonotonicGuard<uint32_t>::IsNewer(msg.seq)` — stale arrivals are silently discarded. `MonotonicGuard` handles `uint32_t` rollover correctly via signed-difference comparison.

## Timer

`dmq::util::Timer` is a non-template class providing one-shot or periodic callbacks. All timers share a global intrusive linked list; expiration is checked by calling `Timer::ProcessTimers()` from a periodic context.

### Key members

- `dmq::Signal<void()> OnExpired` — signal emitted when the timer fires; connect delegates to receive notifications
- `void Start(dmq::Duration timeout, bool once = false)` — start the timer; `once = true` fires once then disables, `once = false` (default) repeats
- `void Stop()` — stop the timer; removal from the list is deferred to the next `ProcessTimers()` call
- `bool Enabled()` — returns whether the timer is currently active
- `static dmq::TimePoint GetNow()` — current time from `dmq::Clock` (the port's monotonic clock)

### ProcessTimers()

```cpp
static void Timer::ProcessTimers();
```

Must be called periodically, from a main loop or a high-priority task. The timer list itself is guarded by `Timer::GetLock()`, a `dmq::CriticalSection` (interrupt masking on RTOS and bare-metal ports, resolved per port in `DelegateOpt.h`), and `Start()`/`Stop()` take only that lock. `ProcessTimers()` then copies each expired timer's subscribers under `Timer::GetProcessLock()`, a `dmq::RecursiveMutex`, which can lock OS mutexes and allocate. So:

| Port | Call `ProcessTimers()` from a hardware ISR? |
|---|---|
| Bare metal / no RTOS (`DMQ_THREAD_NONE`), ARM or RISC-V | Yes (e.g. `SysTick_Handler`) |
| Every RTOS port (FreeRTOS, ThreadX, Zephyr, CMSIS-RTOS2, NuttX) | No — call it from a task (OS mutexes can't be taken in an ISR) |
| Desktop (stdlib/Win32/POSIX/Qt) | No — call it from a thread |

Implementation per port and how each was verified: see the ISR-Safe Locking section of [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md).

It checks every active timer, collects expired timers, then invokes their `OnExpired` signals **outside the lock** to prevent deadlocks. Frequency must be shorter than the shortest timer period; 5–10 ms is typical.

**ProcessTimers() must never block.** Scenarios that cause blocking or faulting:

1. A timer callback dispatches to a thread whose queue is full and the thread uses `FullPolicy::TIMEOUT` — stalls up to the timeout. Fix: use `FullPolicy::FAULT` or `DROP` on threads that receive timer dispatches, or `MakeTimerDelegate()` (below).
2. A `DelegateAsyncWait` is connected to `OnExpired` — blocks indefinitely. Never do this.
3. A synchronous callback connected to `OnExpired` runs slowly — blocks for its duration. Keep sync callbacks fast or dispatch work asynchronously.
4. Calling `ProcessTimers()` from a hardware ISR on any port except bare metal — it takes OS mutexes there. See the table above.

### Recommended call sites

```cpp
// Bare metal (DMQ_THREAD_NONE) only — hardware ISR is safe
extern "C" void SysTick_Handler() {
    dmq::util::Timer::ProcessTimers();
}

// Every RTOS port, and desktop — a high-priority task or thread
void TimerTask(void*) {
    while (true) {
        dmq::util::Timer::ProcessTimers();
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(10));
    }
}
```

### Configuration constants

Defaults live in `delegate/DelegateMQConfig_Default.h`; override them in your own `DelegateMQConfig.h` (seed it from `DelegateMQConfig_Template.h`). Each is exposed in code as a `dmq::` constant (e.g. `DMQ_MAX_TIMER_EXPIRED` → `dmq::MAX_TIMER_EXPIRED`).

- `DMQ_MAX_TIMER_EXPIRED` (16) — timers collected per `ProcessTimers()` pass; a larger backlog is drained in further bounded passes, not by allocating
- `DMQ_MAX_WATCHDOG_THREADS` (16) — maximum threads registered for watchdog monitoring

## Best Practices for Constrained Systems (STM32, ESP32, etc.)

For applications running on MCUs with limited RAM (e.g., 64KB–512KB), follow these guidelines to ensure deterministic performance and prevent heap exhaustion:

1. **Enable `DMQ_ALLOCATOR`**: This is the most critical step. It replaces the standard `malloc`/`free` with DelegateMQ's fixed-block allocator for all internal library structures (DataBus topics, connections, async messages). This eliminates fragmentation and makes memory usage predictable.
2. **Prefer Class Member Delegates**: Use `dmq::MakeDelegate(this, &Class::Method)` instead of capturing lambdas for internal plumbing or long-lived connections. Member function delegates are fixed-size and never allocate, whereas a lambda is stored in a `std::function` and a large capture can silently exceed its small-buffer optimization and allocate.
3. **Be Mindful of Async Arguments**: When using `DelegateAsync`, every argument is copied: by-value arguments into the message, the data behind reference and pointer arguments to the heap. 
    - **Avoid**: Passing large structs or strings by value.
    - **Prefer**: Passing by `const T&` if the object's lifetime is guaranteed (e.g., a singleton or global).
    - **Prefer**: Using `std::shared_ptr<T>` to share ownership; only the smart pointer is copied, not the underlying data.
4. **Tune capacities in `DelegateMQConfig.h`**: queue sizes (`DMQ_DEFAULT_QUEUE_SIZE`), `DMQ_MAX_PARTICIPANTS`, `DMQ_MAX_TIMER_EXPIRED`, etc. Defaults and descriptions are in `delegate/DelegateMQConfig_Default.h`.

## Lambdas

Lambdas are fully supported in application code: pass one directly to `dmq::MakeDelegate()`, sync or async. It is stored in a `std::function`, so a large capture can allocate; on constrained targets see item 2 above. (Library internals avoid capturing lambdas; see [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md).)

## MakeTimerDelegate

`dmq::util::MakeTimerDelegate()` creates a timer-safe async delegate that prevents queue flooding. Unlike `MakeDelegate()`, it guarantees **at most one message in flight** to the target thread at any time — additional timer ticks are silently dropped while the previous dispatch is still pending. Use it whenever connecting a delegate to `Timer::OnExpired`.

### Signatures

```cpp
// Member function, raw pointer
template <typename TClass>
TimerDelegate MakeTimerDelegate(
    TClass* obj,
    void (TClass::*method)(),
    dmq::IThread& thread,
    dmq::UnicastDelegate<void()> onStuck = dmq::UnicastDelegate<void()>(),  // optional: called if dispatch is stuck
    dmq::Duration stuckTimeout = dmq::Duration(0));                        // optional: how long before "stuck"

// Member function, shared_ptr owner (lifetime-safe)
template <typename TClass>
TimerDelegate MakeTimerDelegate(
    std::shared_ptr<TClass> obj,
    void (TClass::*method)(),
    dmq::IThread& thread,
    dmq::UnicastDelegate<void()> onStuck = dmq::UnicastDelegate<void()>(),
    dmq::Duration stuckTimeout = dmq::Duration(0));

// Free function / static member: void(*func)()
// Lambda or other callable
template <typename F>
TimerDelegate MakeTimerDelegate(
    F&& func,
    dmq::IThread& thread,
    dmq::UnicastDelegate<void()> onStuck = dmq::UnicastDelegate<void()>(),
    dmq::Duration stuckTimeout = dmq::Duration(0));
```

Each member-function form also has a `const` method overload (`const TClass*` or `std::shared_ptr<TClass>` with `void (TClass::*)() const`). Member and free-function targets are stored as plain delegates; only lambdas/callables are wrapped in a `std::function`.

`onStuck` takes a `dmq::UnicastDelegate<void()>` — build it with `dmq::MakeDelegate()` (e.g. `dmq::MakeDelegate(this, &MyClass::OnThreadStuck)`). Returns a `TimerDelegate` (derives from `dmq::Delegate<void()>`) that can be passed directly to `Timer::OnExpired.Connect()`.

### How it differs from MakeDelegate

| | `MakeDelegate` | `MakeTimerDelegate` |
|---|---|---|
| In-flight messages | Unlimited (one per tick) | At most one |
| Queue flooding | Possible on fast timers | Prevented |
| Blocking (`DelegateAsyncWait`) | Supported | Not supported (always async) |
| Stuck detection | No | Optional via `onStuck` |
| `shared_ptr` target held weakly | Yes | Yes |

### Usage examples

```cpp
// Basic usage — raw pointer
m_conn = m_timer.OnExpired.Connect(
    dmq::util::MakeTimerDelegate(this, &MyClass::OnTick, m_thread));
m_timer.Start(std::chrono::milliseconds(100));

// Shared_ptr owner — target held as weak_ptr; the call is skipped if the
// object is gone by the time the worker thread runs it
auto self = std::make_shared<MyClass>();
auto d = dmq::util::MakeTimerDelegate(self, &MyClass::OnTick, m_thread);
self->m_conn = self->m_timer.OnExpired.Connect(d);

// With stuck detection — onStuck fires from ProcessTimers() context on each
// tick that finds the previous dispatch still pending after stuckTimeout
m_conn = m_timer.OnExpired.Connect(
    dmq::util::MakeTimerDelegate(this, &MyClass::OnTick, m_thread,
        dmq::MakeDelegate(this, &MyClass::OnThreadStuck), std::chrono::seconds(2)));
```

### At-most-one guarantee

Internally, each dispatch carries a `DispatchToken` (a `shared_ptr`); the `TimerDelegate`'s `PacedDispatch` gate keeps only a `weak_ptr` to it. When the timer fires:
- If the previous dispatch is still in flight (token alive), the tick is dropped.
- If the previous dispatch completed, or the target thread rejected it under `FullPolicy::DROP` (token destroyed), the next dispatch is queued.

This prevents a slow handler from causing unbounded queue growth on the target thread, and means `ProcessTimers()` never waits on a `FullPolicy::TIMEOUT` queue while a dispatch is already pending. A `TimerDelegate` is meant to be invoked from a single `ProcessTimers()` context; it is not safe for concurrent invocation.

Disconnecting the connection (or destroying, clearing or reassigning the `TimerDelegate`) cancels a tick it queued that the worker hasn't started: the target is not called. Two cases still run: a tick the worker has already started, and one that `ProcessTimers()` queues while `Disconnect()` runs on another thread (`Signal` emits a snapshot of its connections). So disconnecting alone doesn't make it safe to free a raw-pointer target. Stop the timer, disconnect, and drain the worker (e.g. `ExitThread()`) first, as `NetworkNode::Stop()` does.

## Watchdog

The watchdog is built into every `dmq::os::Thread`. It detects threads that deadlock, spin indefinitely, or become unresponsive. There is no separate Watchdog class — it is an optional feature of `Thread`.

### Enabling the watchdog

Pass a timeout to `CreateThread()`:

```cpp
dmq::os::Thread worker("Worker");
worker.CreateThread(std::chrono::seconds(2));  // 2-second watchdog
```

Without a timeout argument, the watchdog is disabled for that thread.

### How it works

1. **Self-reporting:** The thread's `Process()` loop records `m_lastAliveTime = Timer::GetNow()` at the top of every iteration and again after waking from the queue wait. With a watchdog enabled the queue wait uses a finite timeout (`watchdogTimeout / DMQ_WATCHDOG_HEARTBEAT_DIVISOR`, default 4) so even idle threads loop frequently.
2. **Checking:** the application calls the static `dmq::os::Thread::WatchdogCheckAll()` periodically (e.g. every 100 ms) from its own loop or task — the library does not schedule it, and `ProcessTimers()` does not call it. It reads `m_lastAliveTime` atomically for each registered thread. If `now − lastAlive > watchdogTimeout`, `WatchdogHandler(threadName)` is called.

```cpp
// Highest-priority task (FreeRTOS shown; see example/cellutron for ThreadX/stdlib)
void vWatchdogTask(void*) {
    while (true) {
        dmq::os::Thread::WatchdogCheckAll();
        vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(100));
    }
}
```
3. **Fault:** `WatchdogHandler` is an `extern "C"` stub the application provides. The default triggers a `FAULT` (assert/halt); a custom implementation can log the thread name and initiate system recovery.

### Long-running handlers

If a message handler legitimately runs longer than `watchdogTimeout`, call `ThreadCheck()` inside the handler to reset the alive timestamp:

```cpp
void MyClass::LongHandler() {
    for (auto& item : bigList) {
        process(item);
        m_thread.ThreadCheck();  // keep watchdog satisfied during long work
    }
}
```

### Key methods

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `CreateThread(std::optional<dmq::Duration>)` | Pass a timeout to enable the watchdog and register the thread |
| `static WatchdogCheckAll()` | Check every registered thread; call periodically from the application |
| `ThreadCheck()` | Manually reset the alive timestamp inside a long handler |
| `ExitThread()` | Stops watchdog checks once the thread has finished (a thread that hangs while `ExitThread()` waits is still reported); it stays registered until destroyed |

### Priority requirement

The watchdog only catches a runaway thread if the `WatchdogCheckAll()` caller runs at **higher priority** than the runaway thread. On a single-core RTOS, a CPU-spinning task at equal or higher priority than that caller will starve the watchdog — so call it from the highest-priority task in the system.

Do **not** call `WatchdogCheckAll()` from a hardware ISR: it takes the thread list's `dmq::RecursiveMutex`, an OS mutex that cannot be acquired from interrupt context on any RTOS port.

For maximum reliability, pair the software watchdog with a hardware watchdog (e.g., STM32 IWDG) and kick it from the same loop, right after `WatchdogCheckAll()` returns — that way a stuck or starved watchdog task also triggers a hardware reset.

## Platform and OS Support

Desktop / server: Windows (Win32), Linux (stdlib, or raw pthreads via `DMQ_THREAD_POSIX`), Qt event loop.

Embedded / RTOS: FreeRTOS, ThreadX / NetX, Zephyr, CMSIS-RTOS2, NuttX, bare-metal (ARM Cortex-M and RISC-V), ATfE (picolibc).

For unsupported platforms, implement the `dmq::IThread` interface and the library compiles unchanged.

## Build and Integration

- Include `DelegateMQ.h`; the core is header-only and requires only C++17.
- CMake is the primary build system; it auto-detects the platform and selects defaults.
- As a dependency (FetchContent or `add_subdirectory`): set `DMQ_*` options first, then `target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE DelegateMQ::DelegateMQ)`; the static library target carries the port sources, definitions and include paths.
- For async delegates or DataBus, also compile the `DMQ_PORT_SOURCES` for the target OS/thread port. (`include(DelegateMQ.cmake)` path; `dmq_add_library(<name>)` turns those into a target).
- Without CMake (Keil, IAR, STM32CubeIDE, Makefiles): add `src/delegate-mq` to the include path and compile either `src/DelegateMQ.cpp` or every `.cpp` under `src/delegate-mq` (not both); select ports/options with `#define`s in a `DelegateMQConfig.h` on the include path (copy `delegate/DelegateMQConfig_Template.h`). See `example/sample-projects/no-cmake-integration`.
- Key CMake options: `DMQ_THREAD` (e.g., `DMQ_THREAD_STDLIB`, `DMQ_THREAD_FREERTOS`, `DMQ_THREAD_WIN32`), `DMQ_ALLOCATOR` (fixed-block allocator), `DMQ_ASSERTS`, `DMQ_TOOLS`.

## Diagnostic Tools (DMQ_TOOLS=ON)

Desktop-only (`tools/`), not part of the library. See [TOOLS](tools/TOOLS.md).

- `dmq-spy` — real-time feed of all DataBus messages with topic (substring) filtering. Headless modes `--echo`, `--hz`, `--bw` print to stdout; `--log <file> --log-format text|csv|json`; `--plotjuggler` streams numeric values to PlotJuggler's UDP Server for live plots
- `dmq-monitor` — live network topology dashboard (nodes, IP, uptime, topics)
- `dmq-thread` — per-thread performance dashboard (latency, queue depth)
- `dmq-target` — test source app exercising the Spy and Node bridges (used for tool/integration testing, not a diagnostic console)
- Only one tool can listen on a unicast UDP port; a second one exits with an error. Multicast (`--multicast`) allows several.

Bridges an application links in (`tools/bridge/`):

- `spy/SpyBridge` — mirrors the node's DataBus traffic to `dmq-spy` over UDP (needs stringifiers via `DataBus::RegisterStringifier`)
- `node/NodeBridge` — heartbeats and thread stats to `dmq-monitor` / `dmq-thread`
- `common/JsonTopics` — shared JSON bridge layer: declare once which topics to expose (`Expose<T>(topic, toJson, {latched, reliable})`) and which commands to accept (`Accept<T>(topic, fromJson)`); every JSON bridge serves that set
- `mqtt/MqttBridge` — MQTT gateway for JsonTopics: `<prefix>/<topic>` JSON payloads, commands on `<prefix>/<topic>/set`, retained latched state, `<prefix>/online` Last Will. Standard MQTT for any MQTT client; built with `dmq_add_mqtt_bridge(target)` from `tools/bridge/mqtt/MqttBridge.cmake` (Paho MQTT C)
- `tools/wireshark/dmq.lua` — Wireshark dissector for the DelegateMQ UDP/TCP header

## Cross-Language Interop

`interop/native` builds `DmqInterop`, a C API over DelegateMQ transports with reliable sends (ACK + retry, per-message `ACKED` / `TIMEOUT` / `DELIVERY_FAILED` status via `DmqInterop_RegisterStatusCallback`; `DmqInterop_Send` returns the sequence number). `interop/python` (`dmq_databus.DmqDataBus`) and `interop/csharp` (`DelegateMQ.Interop.DmqDataBus`) wrap it. Cross-language messages use MessagePack (`MSGPACK_DEFINE` in C++). See [INTEROP](docs/INTEROP.md).

## Comparison to Alternatives

DelegateMQ differs from Qt signals (requires moc, Qt base class, Qt event loop), Boost.Signals2 (no async delivery, no remote, no embedded support), DDS (no IDL, no code gen, tiny footprint), and gRPC (no local/async mode, requires protobuf). DelegateMQ is the only option in this space that provides sync, async, and remote invocation in a single API with embedded/RTOS support. See [COMPARISON](docs/COMPARISON.md) for the full comparison.

## Contributor Conventions (Modifying the Library)

Code under `src/delegate-mq/` follows strict rules because the library targets embedded/RTOS platforms: no heap in library internals (`std::array`, `xmap`, `xlist`, `xstring` instead of std containers), allocator and platform types selected only through `DelegateOpt.h`, portable `dmq::` locking/thread/clock types, tunable limits as `DMQ_*` config macros, `BAD_ALLOC()`/`DMQ_ASSERT` instead of `throw`/`assert`, and self-guarding `.cpp` files. The complete, authoritative rules are in [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md).
